steps.body: The standard-algorithm diagram makes regrouping visible. When 4 × 3 makes 12 ones, 2 ones stay in the ones place and 1 ten moves left before the tens are multiplied.
steps.narration: The standard-algorithm diagram makes regrouping visible. When 4 × 3 makes 12 ones, 2 ones stay in the ones place and 1 ten moves left before the tens are multiplied.

steps.body: Build the model and describe what its values show.

widget.prompt: Work 487 × 6 in columns and watch each carry land.

commonResults.feedback: 2,882 dropped the carry the tens column produced — those forty units never arrived.
Two carries went missing on the way left; each stranded carry costs exactly its own value.

widget.fallbackFeedback: Multiply from the ones place toward the left. Regroup every full bundle into the next place, then include it in that column's product.
widget.successFeedback: 487 × 6 = 2922. The proposed product rebuilds every place correctly.

predict.prompt: In 487 × 6, the ones give 7 × 6 = 42. What stays in the ones column?
predict.reveal: A column holds one digit. Forty-two is 4 tens and 2 ones — the 2 stays, the 4 tens move left.

cml.actionGoal: Split a factor into places, build each piece, and reassemble the whole for g4m regroup.
invariants: Splitting a factor never changes the product: every piece of the split multiplies the other factor, and the pieces add back to exactly the same total, which is what makes g4m regroup decomposable at all.
misconceptions: Adding only some of the partial products, dropping or inventing a zero when factors carry tens, or letting a remainder reach or exceed the divisor.
cml.counterfactualPrompt: If one partial product were left out, exactly how much of the total would go missing?

widget.prompt: Use an area model for 42 × 3. What is the product?

commonErrors.feedback: That is only the tens piece (40 × 3). The ones piece 2 × 3 still has to be added on.
That is only the ones piece. The 40 in 42 contributes 40 × 3 as well.
